Global boundedness and stabilization for a three-component reaction-diffusion model with dual-dependent motility

Hai-Yang Jin Address: School of Mathematics, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou 510640, P.R. China Email address: mahyjin@scut.edu.cn and Jingyi Mai Address: School of Mathematics, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou 510640, P.R. China Email address: majymai@163.com
Abstract.

In this paper, we consider the initial-boundary value problem of a three-component reaction-diffusion system with dual-dependent motility (which depends on both vv and mm):

{ut=Δ⁡[γ⁡(v,m)​u]+α​u​m,x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δ​v−v+(θ1+θ2​m)​u,x∈Ω,t>0,mt=Δ​m−u​m,x∈Ω,t>0,∇(uγ(v,m))⋅ν=∇v⋅ν=∇m⋅ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,(u,v,m)​(x,0)=(u0,v0,m0)​(x),x∈Ω,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta[\gamma(v,m)u]+\alpha um,&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ v_{t}=\Delta v-v+(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}m)u,&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ m_{t}=\Delta m-um,&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ \nabla(u\gamma(v,m))\cdot\nu=\nabla v\cdot\nu=\nabla m\cdot\nu=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,~t>0,\\ (u,v,m)(x,0)=(u_{0},v_{0},m_{0})(x),&x\in\Omega,\end{cases} (*)

where Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} is a bounded domain with a smooth boundary. Here α\alpha, θ1\theta_{1} and θ2\theta_{2} are non-negative constants, and ν\nu denotes the outward unit normal vector on ∂Ω\partial\Omega. The random motility function γ⁡(v,m)\gamma(v,m), depending on both the chemical concentration vv and the nutrient level mm, satisfies:

  • •

    γ⁡(v,m)∈C3​([0,∞)×[0,∞))\gamma(v,m)\in C^{3}\left([0,\infty)\times[0,\infty)\right), γ⁡(v,m)>0\gamma(v,m)>0, γv​(v,m)≤0\gamma_{v}(v,m)\leq 0, γm​(v,m)≥0\gamma_{m}(v,m)\geq 0 on [0,∞)×[0,∞)[0,\infty)\times[0,\infty); moreover, limv→+∞γ⁡(v,m)=0\lim\limits_{v\to+\infty}\gamma(v,m)=0 for any m≥0m\geq 0.

For θ1=0\theta_{1}=0, we first establish the existence of global classical solutions with uniform-in-time bounds for the system (*), and further prove that the solution (u,v,m)(u,v,m) converges to the constant steady state (u∗,0,0)(u_{*},0,0) as t→∞t\to\infty, where u∗=1|Ω|​(‖u0‖L1+α​‖m0‖L1)u_{*}=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\left(\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}}+\alpha\|m_{0}\|_{L^{1}}\right). For θ1>0\theta_{1}>0, we demonstrate the global boundedness of solutions under appropriate decay conditions on γ⁡(v,m)\gamma(v,m). We further show that there exists θ∗>0\theta_{*}>0 such that if 0<θ1≤θ∗0<\theta_{1}\leq\theta_{*}, all solutions converge to (u∗,θ1​u∗,0)(u_{*},\theta_{1}u_{*},0) as t→∞t\to\infty with u∗u_{*} defined as above.

Our analysis employs refined energy estimates, moser iteration techniques, and careful exploitation of the structural properties of γ⁡(v,m)\gamma(v,m). These results characterize the solution behavior in both cases (θ1=0\theta_{1}=0 and θ1>0\theta_{1}>0), highlighting the crucial role of dual-dependent motility in the system’s long-term dynamics.

Key words and phrases: 
Density-dependent motion, global existence, global stabilization, uniform-in-time bound

35A01, 35B40, 35B44, 35K57, 35Q92, 92C17

1. Introduction

In this paper, we consider the initial-boundary value problem for the following three-component reaction-diffusion system with density-dependent motility

{ut=Δ⁡[γ⁡(v,m)​u]+α​u​m,x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δ​v−v+(θ1+θ2​m)​u,x∈Ω,t>0,mt=Δ​m−u​m,x∈Ω,t>0,∇(uγ(v,m))⋅ν=∇v⋅ν=∇m⋅ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,(u,v,m)​(x,0)=(u0,v0,m0)​(x),x∈Ω,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta[\gamma(v,m)u]+\alpha um,&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ v_{t}=\Delta v-v+(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}m)u,&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ m_{t}=\Delta m-um,&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ \nabla(u\gamma(v,m))\cdot\nu=\nabla v\cdot\nu=\nabla m\cdot\nu=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,~t>0,\\ (u,v,m)(x,0)=(u_{0},v_{0},m_{0})(x),&x\in\Omega,\end{cases} (1.1)

where Ω⊂ℝn​(n≥1)\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}(n\geq 1) is a bounded domain with smooth boundary and ν\nu stands for the outward unit normal vector on ∂Ω\partial\Omega. The parameters α≥0\alpha\geq 0 and θ1,θ2≥0\theta_{1},\theta_{2}\geq 0. The motility response function γ⁡(v,m)\gamma(v,m) depends on both chemical concentration vv and the nutrient nn, exhibiting chemical-immobilizing and resource-mobilizing properties in the sense that

γv​(v,m)≤0andγm​(v,m)≥0.\gamma_{v}(v,m)\leq 0\ \ \mathrm{and}\ \ \gamma_{m}(v,m)\geq 0.

Such kind of dual-dependent motility function γ⁡(v,m)\gamma(v,m) was first derived in [6] by considering dweller-wanderer interactions, where the organisms adjust their movement patterns (e.g., velocity, turning frequency, residence time) in response to dual environmental gradients: resource availability and pheromone concentration. This regulation hinges on two opposing yet complementary responses, which collectively optimize the trade-off between local exploitation (by dwellers) and global exploration (by wanderers) in a population. For the system (1.1), existing results [36] primarily focus on simplified cases where the motility function γ\gamma depends exclusively on a single variable: either γ⁡(v,m)=ϕ⁡(v)\gamma(v,m)=\phi(v) or γ⁡(v,m)=φ⁡(m)\gamma(v,m)=\varphi(m).

Case 1: γ⁡(v,m)=ϕ⁡(v)\gamma(v,m)=\phi(v). In this case, when θ2=0\theta_{2}=0, the system (1.1) reduces to the following form:

{ut=Δ⁡[ϕ⁡(v)​u]+α​u​m,x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δ​v−v+θ1​u,x∈Ω,t>0,mt=Δ​m−u​m,x∈Ω,t>0,∇(ϕ(v)u)⋅ν=∇v⋅ν=∇m⋅ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,(u,v,m)​(x,0)=(u0,v0,m0)​(x),x∈Ω,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta[\phi(v)u]+\alpha um,&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ v_{t}=\Delta v-v+\theta_{1}u,&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ m_{t}=\Delta m-um,&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ \nabla(\phi(v)u)\cdot\nu=\nabla v\cdot\nu=\nabla m\cdot\nu=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,~t>0,\\ (u,v,m)(x,0)=(u_{0},v_{0},m_{0})(x),&x\in\Omega,\end{cases} (1.2)

which was first proposed in [25] to gain a quantitative understanding of the periodic strip pattern formation. For the system (1.2), the global existence, uniform boundedness, and stabilization of classical solutions have been intensively investigated recently by virtue of two distinct methods: energy estimate [29, 17, 18] and comparison method [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15]. More precisely, when n=2n=2 and α=0\alpha=0, the first result on the global boundedness of classical solution for the system (1.2) was obtained by Tao and Winkler [29] under the assumption that 0<ϕ0≤ϕ⁡(v)≤ϕ10<\phi_{0}\leq\phi(v)\leq\phi_{1} by using dual arguments. Based on the ingenious comparison method, Fujie and Jiang [12] relax the assumption 0<ϕ0≤ϕ⁡(v)≤ϕ10<\phi_{0}\leq\phi(v)\leq\phi_{1} and establish global existence for any positive, non-increasing motility function ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v) that converges to zero at infinity, even allowing the function to vanish asymptotically. Moreover, for any non-increasing motility function decaying slower than any negative exponential function at infinity, the uniform-in-time bound of classical solution was obtained [1, 11]. If ϕ⁡(v)=e−χ​v\phi(v)=e^{-\chi v} for χ>0\chi>0, a critical mass phenomenon was found [5, 10, 12, 18] in the sense that if ∫Ωu0​𝑑x<4​πχ​θ1\int_{\Omega}u_{0}dx<\frac{4\pi}{\chi\theta_{1}}, the solution with uniform-in-time bound exists, while the solution will blow up at infinity time if ∫Ωu0​𝑑x>4​πχ​θ1\int_{\Omega}u_{0}dx>\frac{4\pi}{\chi\theta_{1}}.

For higher dimensions (n≥3n\geq 3), it has been proved that the system (1.2) with α=0\alpha=0 has a unique global classical solution for arbitrary positive motility function [13]. The uniform-in-time boundedness of classical solution was also studied extensively for both the simplify parabolic-elliptic case [1, 11, 14] or the full parabolic-parabolic case [11, 12]. This results imply that ϕ⁡(s)∼s−k\phi(s)\sim s^{-k} as s→∞s\to\infty with any k<nn−2k<\frac{n}{n-2} seems to the optimal condition for the existence of global classical of solution with uniform-in time bound when n≥3n\geq 3. The results on global existence, uniformly boundedness and stabilization of constant steady state also been extended to the case α>0\alpha>0, see [17, 12]. At last, we should mention that except the global boundedness and stabilization of classical solution for the system (1.2), there also some results on the weak solution [8, 29]. There also some interesting results on the system (1.2) with logistic growth including boundedness [10, 16], non-constant steady state [31, 27] and traveling wave [23].

Case 2: γ⁡(v,m)=φ⁡(m)\gamma(v,m)=\varphi(m). In this case, the component vv decouples from u,mu,m and hence the system (1.1) becomes

{ut=Δ⁡[φ⁡(m)​u]+α​u​m,x∈Ω,t>0,mt=Δ​m−u​m,x∈Ω,t>0,∇(φ(m)u)⋅ν=∇m⋅ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,(u,m)​(x,0)=(u0,m0)​(x),x∈Ω.\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta[\varphi(m)u]+\alpha um,&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ m_{t}=\Delta m-um,&x\in\Omega,~t>0,\\ \nabla(\varphi(m)u)\cdot\nu=\nabla m\cdot\nu=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,~t>0,\\ (u,m)(x,0)=(u_{0},m_{0})(x),&x\in\Omega.\end{cases} (1.3)

The model (1.3) has been used to describe the bacterial populations how adjust their motility in response to the concentration of surrounding nutrients consumed upon contact. For instance, motility may increase under starvation conditions [7] or decrease when nutrients are scarce, such as in poor agar environments [22]. Compared with chemotaxis-production interaction system (1.2), few results are available for the system (1.3) due to the lack of some favorable structural properties. The solution behaviors of (1.3) depend on the fact that φ⁡(m)\varphi(m) is degenerate or not. More precisely, if φ′​(m)≤0\varphi^{\prime}(m)\leq 0, the system (1.3) can be viewed as the simplest predator–prey system with density-dependent motility [20, 19]. If 1≤n≤21\leq n\leq 2, it has been proved in [21, 32] that the system (1.3) has a unique global classical solution (u,m)(u,m), which converges to the constant steady state (u∗,0)(u_{*},0) with u∗=1|Ω|​∫Ωu0​𝑑x+α|Ω|​∫Ωm0​𝑑xu_{*}=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}u_{0}dx+\frac{\alpha}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}m_{0}dx. The results obtained in [21, 32, 24] are based on the fact φ⁡(m)\varphi(m) is strictly positive throughout [0,∞)[0,\infty) and hence non-degenerate occurs. In contrast to the case φ′​(m)≤0\varphi^{\prime}(m)\leq 0, the solution behavior is much more complex due to the possible degeneracy of φ⁡(m)\varphi(m). In fact, if φ⁡(m)>0\varphi(m)>0 but φ⁡(0)=0\varphi(0)=0, the global classical solution of the system (1.3) still exist in the case of 1≤n≤21\leq n\leq 2, which however will approach a non-constant steady state (u∞,0)(u_{\infty},0) as t→∞t\to\infty when m0m_{0} is appropriately small [35]. These results in [21, 32, 24] imply that the degeneracy of signal-dependent motility plays an important role for the existence of non-constant large-time patterns in related taxis-consumption systems. Beyond the existence of global classical solution for the system (1.3) in lower dimensions (1≤n≤21\leq n\leq 2), the existence of global very weak solution for any dimensions has also been established in [24, 34] for any ϕ∈C3​([0,∞))\phi\in C^{3}([0,\infty)) satisfying φ>0\varphi>0 on [0,∞)[0,\infty).

To our knowledge, there is few result on the chemotaxis model with motility response function γ⁡(v,m)\gamma(v,m) depending on both chemical concentration vv and the nutrient mm. In this paper, we assume that the motility function γ⁡(v,m)\gamma(v,m) satisfies the following properties:

  • (H1)

    γ⁡(v,m)∈C3​([0,∞)×[0,∞))\gamma(v,m)\in C^{3}([0,\infty)\times[0,\infty)), γ⁡(v,m)>0\gamma(v,m)>0 and γv​(v,m)≤0\gamma_{v}(v,m)\leq 0, γm​(v,m)≥0\gamma_{m}(v,m)\geq 0 on [0,∞)×[0,∞)[0,\infty)\times[0,\infty). Moreover, for any m≥0m\geq 0, it holds that

    limv→+∞γ⁡(v,m)=0.\lim\limits_{v\to+\infty}\gamma(v,m)=0.

In this paper, we aim to address several fundamental questions regarding the behavior of solutions to the three-component reaction-diffusion system with a density-dependent motility function γ⁡(v,m)\gamma(v,m) that depends on both the chemical concentration vv and the nutrient mm. Specifically, we investigate the conditions on γ⁡(v,m)\gamma(v,m) under which solutions exist globally in time, whether these solutions stabilize to constant or non-constant steady states as time evolves, and how the interplay between chemical sensing and nutrient sensing influences the formation of spatial patterns. These questions are motivated by the need to extend previous studies that focused on simplified cases where γ\gamma depends solely on vv or mm, and to provide a more comprehensive understanding of systems where the motility is regulated by multiple environmental factors.

Throughout this paper, we assume that the initial value satisfies

(u0,v0,m0)∈[W1,∞(Ω)]3,u0≥0,u0≢0,m0≥0,v0>0inΩ¯.(u_{0},v_{0},m_{0})\in[W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)]^{3},\quad u_{0}\geq 0,\quad u_{0}\not\equiv 0,\quad m_{0}\geq 0,\quad v_{0}>0\quad\text{in}\ \bar{\Omega}. (1.4)

Next, we will investigate the global boundedness and large time behavior of classical solutions to (1.1) for two distinct cases: θ1=0\theta_{1}=0 and θ1>0\theta_{1}>0. If θ1=0\theta_{1}=0, then we have the following results on the global dynamics for the solution behavior.

Theorem 1.1 (Boundedness and stabilization: θ1=0\theta_{1}=0).

Let Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be a bounded domain with smooth boundary and θ1=0\theta_{1}=0. Suppose that γ\gamma satisfies the assumption (H1), and that the initial data (u0,v0,m0)(u_{0},v_{0},m_{0}) satisfies (1.4). Then the system (1.1) has a unique non-negative global classical solution (u,v,m)∈[C⁡(Ω¯×[0,∞))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,∞))]3(u,v,m)\in[C(\bar{\Omega}\times[0,\infty))\cap C^{2,1}(\bar{\Omega}\times(0,\infty))]^{3} satisfying

‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,∞+‖m⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,∞≤C,\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|v(\cdot,t)\|_{W^{1,\infty}}+\|m(\cdot,t)\|_{W^{1,\infty}}\leq C,

where C>0C>0 is a constant independent of tt. Moreover, it holds that

limt→∞(‖u⁡(⋅,t)−u∗‖L∞+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞+‖m⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞)=0,\lim_{t\to\infty}(\|u(\cdot,t)-u_{*}\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|v(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|m(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}})=0,

where u∗=1|Ω|​(‖u0‖L1+α​‖m0‖L1)u_{*}=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}(\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}}+\alpha\|m_{0}\|_{L^{1}}).

Remark 1.1.

The results in Theorem 1.1 imply that the solution will not blow up in two-dimensional spaces and no pattern formation occurs if the chemical signal produced by food.

Remark 1.2.

In Theorem 1.1, we assume that γ⁡(v,m)∈C3​([0,∞)×[0,∞))\gamma(v,m)\in C^{3}([0,\infty)\times[0,\infty)). However, when θ1=0\theta_{1}=0, from Theorem 1.1, we know that vv converges to zero as t→∞t\to\infty. This raises an interesting problem: what can be said about the global dynamics for the case γ⁡(v,m)=m/vk\gamma(v,m)=m/v^{k}?

Remark 1.3.

In Theorem 1.1, we only establish the global existence and boundedness of solutions in two-dimensional spaces. An intriguing open question is whether we can derive the global boundedness of solutions for the system (1.1) with θ1=0\theta_{1}=0 in higher dimensions.

If θ1>0\theta_{1}>0, the behavior of solutions exhibits distinct characteristics. We now elaborate on our findings regarding the global boundedness and stabilization of solutions for the system (1.1) with θ1>0\theta_{1}>0.

Theorem 1.2 (Boundedness and stabilization: θ1>0\theta_{1}>0).

Let Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be a bounded domain with smooth boundary and θ1>0\theta_{1}>0. If γ\gamma satisfies the assumption (H1) and there exists χ>0\chi>0 such that

lim infs→+∞eχ​s​γ​(s,m)>0,for all​m≥0,\liminf_{s\to+\infty}e^{\chi s}\gamma(s,m)>0,\quad\text{for all}\ m\geq 0, (1.5)

and the initial data (u0,v0,m0)(u_{0},v_{0},m_{0}) satisfies (1.4) with

‖u0+α​m0‖L1<4​πχ⁡(θ1+θ2​‖m0‖L∞).\|u_{0}+\alpha m_{0}\|_{L^{1}}<\frac{4\pi}{\chi(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\|m_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}})}.

Then the system (1.1) has a unique global classical solution with uniform-in-time bound. Moreover, there exists a constant θ∗>0\theta_{*}>0 such that if 0<θ1≤θ∗0<\theta_{1}\leq\theta_{*}, then

limt→∞(‖u⁡(⋅,t)−u∗‖L∞+‖v⁡(⋅,t)−θ1​u∗‖L∞+‖m⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞)=0,\lim_{t\to\infty}\left(\|u(\cdot,t)-u_{*}\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|v(\cdot,t)-\theta_{1}u_{*}\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|m(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\right)=0,

where u∗=1|Ω|​(‖u0‖L1+α​‖m0‖L1)u_{*}=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}(\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}}+\alpha\|m_{0}\|_{L^{1}}).

In particular, if γ\gamma satisfies the assumptions (H1) and (1.5) for any χ>0\chi>0, then the system (1.1) still has a unique classical solution with uniform-in-time bound for any initial data (u0,v0,m0)(u_{0},v_{0},m_{0}) satisfying (1.4).

Remark 1.4.

Comparing the results in Theorem 1.1 (θ1=0\theta_{1}=0) and Theorem 1.2 (θ1>0\theta_{1}>0), we observe that the presence of chemical production (θ1>0\theta_{1}>0) leads to different asymptotic behavior, with the chemical concentration vv stabilizing to θ1​u∗\theta_{1}u_{*} rather than zero.

2. Local existence and Preliminaries

We first establish the existence of local solutions to (1.1) by employing the Schauder fixed point theorem along with the parabolic regularity theory [16] or the Amann’s theorem [4, 3]. For brevity, we omit the details of the proof.

Lemma 2.1 (Local existence).

Let Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be a bounded domain with smooth boundary. Assume that γ\gamma satisfies (H1) and the initial data (u0,v0,m0)(u_{0},v_{0},m_{0}) satisfies (1.4). Then there exists Tmax∈(0,∞]T_{\max}\in(0,\infty] such that the problem (1.1) has a unique non-negative classical solution (u,v,m)∈[C⁡(Ω¯×[0,Tmax))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,Tmax))]3(u,v,m)\in[C(\bar{\Omega}\times[0,T_{\max}))\cap C^{2,1}(\bar{\Omega}\times(0,T_{\max}))]^{3}. If Tmax<∞T_{\max}<\infty, then

lim supt↗Tmax‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞=∞.\limsup_{t\nearrow T_{\max}}\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}}=\infty.

With the local existence of solution in hand, we establish some basic estimates of solutions for the system (1.1).

Lemma 2.2.

Let (u,v,m)(u,v,m) be the solution of (1.1) obtained in Lemma 2.1, then we have

0<‖u0‖L1≤‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L1≤‖u0+α​m0‖L1,for all​t∈[0,Tmax),0<\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}}\leq\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{1}}\leq\|u_{0}+\alpha m_{0}\|_{L^{1}},\quad\text{for all}\ t\in[0,T_{\max}), (2.1)

and

0≤m⁡(x,t)≤‖m0‖L∞:=m∗,(x,t)∈Ω¯×[0,Tmax),0\leq m(x,t)\leq\|m_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}:=m^{*},\quad(x,t)\in\bar{\Omega}\times[0,T_{\max}), (2.2)

as well as

‖m⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​is decreasing in​t.\|m(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\ \text{is decreasing in}\ t. (2.3)
Proof.

Integrating the first equation of (1.1) and using the non-negativity of uu and mm, we derive

dd​t​∫Ωu=α​∫Ωu​m,\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}u=\alpha\int_{\Omega}um, (2.4)

which gives

‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L1≥‖u0‖L1>0.\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{1}}\geq\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}}>0. (2.5)

On the other hand, multiplying the third equation of (1.1) by α\alpha, and integrating it by parts and adding it to (2.4), one has

dd​t​∫Ω(u+α​m)=0\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}(u+\alpha m)=0

and hence

‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L1≤∫Ω(u+α​m)=∫Ω(u0+α​m0).\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{1}}\leq\int_{\Omega}(u+\alpha m)=\int_{\Omega}(u_{0}+\alpha m_{0}). (2.6)

Then the combination of (2.5) and (2.6) gives (2.1).

Applying the parabolic comparison principle and noting the non-negativity of mm and uu, we obtain (2.2) directly.

At last, we shall employ the maximum principle to prove (2.3). For any fixed t0∈[0,Tmax)t_{0}\in[0,T_{\max}) and (x,t)∈Ω×[0,Tmax−t0)(x,t)\in\Omega\times[0,T_{\max}-t_{0}), we set

z⁡(x,t)=m⁡(x,t+t0)−‖m⁡(⋅,t0)‖L∞.z(x,t)=m(x,t+t_{0})-\|m(\cdot,t_{0})\|_{L^{\infty}}.

Then we can check that zz satisfies

{zt−Δ​z+u​z≤0,x∈Ω,t∈(0,Tmax−t0),∇z⋅ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t∈(0,Tmax−t0),z⁡(x,0)=m⁡(x,t0)−‖m⁡(⋅,t0)‖L∞≤0,x∈Ω.\left\{\begin{aligned} &z_{t}-\Delta z+uz\leq 0,&&\quad x\in\Omega,\ t\in(0,T_{\max}-t_{0}),\\ &\nabla z\cdot\nu=0,&&\quad x\in\partial\Omega,\ t\in(0,T_{\max}-t_{0}),\\ &z(x,0)=m(x,t_{0})-\|m(\cdot,t_{0})\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq 0,&&\quad x\in\Omega.\end{aligned}\right.

Thus, invoking the maximum principle, we deduce that

m(x,t+t0)≤∥m(⋅,t0)∥L∞for(x,t)∈Ω×[0,Tmax−t0),m(x,t+t_{0})\leq\|m(\cdot,t_{0})\|_{L^{\infty}}\ \ \ \mathrm{for}\ \ (x,t)\in\Omega\times[0,T_{\max}-t_{0}), (2.7)

which gives (2.3), due to the arbitrary of t0t_{0}. ∎

The following lemma has been proven in [9, Lemma 2.3] and [30, Lemma 3.3].

Lemma 2.3.

Let Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be a bounded domain. Assume that f∈C⁡(Ω¯)f\in C(\bar{\Omega}) is a non-negative function satisfying ‖f‖L1=Λ>0\|f\|_{L^{1}}=\Lambda>0. If z∈C2​(Ω¯)z\in C^{2}(\bar{\Omega}) is a solution to

{−Δ​z+z=f,x∈Ω,∂z∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω,\begin{cases}-\Delta z+z=f,&\quad x\in\Omega,\\ \frac{\partial z}{\partial\nu}=0,&\quad x\in\partial\Omega,\\ \end{cases}

then one has

z≥C1​‖f‖L1>0in​Ω,z\geq C_{1}\|f\|_{L^{1}}>0\quad\text{in}\ \Omega, (2.8)

and

‖z‖Lq≤C2​‖f‖L1,for​ 1≤q<∞\|z\|_{L^{q}}\leq C_{2}\|f\|_{L^{1}},\quad\text{for}\ 1\leq q<\infty (2.9)

as well as

∫Ωeσ​z​𝑑x≤C3​eC4​σ​Λ,ifσ<4​πΛ,\int_{\Omega}e^{\sigma z}dx\leq C_{3}e^{C_{4}\sigma\Lambda},\ \ \mathrm{if}\ \ \sigma<\frac{4\pi}{\Lambda}, (2.10)

where Ci​(i=1,2,3,4)C_{i}(i=1,2,3,4) are positive constants.

Proof.

The proof of (2.8) can be found in [9, Lemma 2.3]. Next, using the representation of resolvents and the smoothing estimates for Neumann semigroup, we derive

‖z‖Lq≤c1​‖(I−Δ)−1​f‖Lq≤c2​∫0∞e−t​‖et​Δ​f‖Lq​𝑑t≤c3​(∫0∞e−t​t−1+1q​𝑑t)​‖f‖L1,\|z\|_{L^{q}}\leq c_{1}\|(I-\Delta)^{-1}f\|_{L^{q}}\leq c_{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t}\|e^{t\Delta}f\|_{L^{q}}dt\leq c_{3}\left(\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t}t^{-1+\frac{1}{q}}dt\right)\|f\|_{L^{1}},

and then (2.9) follows by noting ∫0∞e−t​t−1+1q​𝑑t≤c4\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t}t^{-1+\frac{1}{q}}dt\leq c_{4} due to 1≤q<+∞1\leq q<+\infty. The estimate (2.10) is proved in [30, Lemma 3.3]. Hence, we complete the proof of Lemma 2.3. ∎

At last, we state a basic lemma will be used to establish the boundedness of solutions.

Lemma 2.4 ([26]).

Let T>0T>0, τ∈(0,T)\tau\in(0,T), a>0a>0 and b>0b>0. Suppose that y:[0,T)→[0,∞)y:[0,T)\rightarrow[0,\infty) is absolutely continuous and fulfills

y′​(t)+a​y​(t)≤h⁡(t),for all​t∈(0,T),y^{\prime}(t)+ay(t)\leq h(t),\quad\text{for all}\ t\in(0,T),

∫tt+τh(s)ds≤b,for allt∈[0,T−τ).\int_{t}^{t+\tau}h(s)ds\leq b,\quad\text{for all}\ t\in[0,T-\tau).

Then

y⁡(t)≤max⁡{y⁡(0)+b,ba​τ+2​b},for all​t∈(0,T).y(t)\leq\max\left\{y(0)+b,\frac{b}{a\tau}+2b\right\},\quad\text{for all}\ t\in(0,T).

Lemma 3.6.

and

3.2. Global stabilization: θ1=0\theta_{1}=0

∫0∞∫Ωu​m<∞\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}um<\infty (3.40)

Lemma 3.9.

Let the conditions in Lemma 3.8 hold. Then there exists a time sequence (tk)k∈ℕ⊂(0,∞)(t_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\subset(0,\infty) satisfying tk→∞t_{k}\to\infty as k→∞k\to\infty such that

∫tktk+1∫Ωm→0ask→∞.\int_{t_{k}}^{t_{k}+1}\int_{\Omega}m\to 0\quad\text{as}\quad k\to\infty. (3.44)
Proof.

∫jj+1∫Ωu​m→0,asj→∞.\int_{j}^{j+1}\int_{\Omega}um\to 0,\quad\text{as}\quad j\to\infty. (3.45)

4. Proof of Theorem 1.2: Boundedness and stabilization with θ1>0\theta_{1}>0

In this section, we shall prove the global boundedness and global stabilization for the system (1.1) with θ1>0\theta_{1}>0 as stated in Theorem 1.2. To this end, we first derive the upper bound for vv in the case of θ1>0\theta_{1}>0 based on the comparison method developed in [15, 10].

4.1. Auxiliary functions and properties

To obtain the lower and upper bound for vv, we first introduce two auxiliary functions ww and SS, and then present some properties of the auxiliary functions as well as the connection between vv and the auxiliary functions ww and SS.

Here the auxiliary function w⁡(x,t)w(x,t) is the unique non-negative solution of the following Helmholtz equation

{−Δ​w+w=u,x∈Ω,t>0,∇w⋅ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0.\begin{cases}-\Delta w+w=u,&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \nabla w\cdot\nu=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,\ t>0.\end{cases} (4.1)

and

S0​(x)≜S⁡(x,0)=𝒜−1​[u0+α​m0]​(x)andw0​(x)≜w⁡(x,0)=𝒜−1​[u0]​(x),S_{0}(x)\triangleq S(x,0)=\mathcal{A}^{-1}[u_{0}+\alpha m_{0}](x)\quad\text{and}\quad w_{0}(x)\triangleq w(x,0)=\mathcal{A}^{-1}[u_{0}](x),

limt→∞(‖u⁡(⋅,t)−u∗‖L2+‖v⁡(⋅,t)−θ1​u∗‖L2)=limt→∞Y⁡(t)=0.\lim_{t\to\infty}(\|u(\cdot,t)-u_{*}\|_{L^{2}}+\|v(\cdot,t)-\theta_{1}u_{*}\|_{L^{2}})=\lim_{t\to\infty}Y(t)=0. (4.70)

Applying the parabolic regularity, we obtain that

‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,∞+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,∞≤c4fort≥1.\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{W^{1,\infty}}+\|v(\cdot,t)\|_{W^{1,\infty}}\leq c_{4}\ \ \mathrm{for}\ \ t\geq 1. (4.71)

Hence, we invoke the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality to conclude (4.62) by (4.70) and (4.71). ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.2: Stabilization.

From (4.61) and Lemma 4.7, we complete the global stabilization of the constant steady state (u∗,θ1​u∗,0)(u_{*},\theta_{1}u_{*},0). ∎
